Text 1

Parents and teachers often assume that a toddler’s play benefits from abundance. A playroom stocked with blocks, puzzles, toy trucks, and pretend-play sets, the reasoning goes, offers far more chances to explore than a sparsely furnished one. If so, surrounding young children with a large and varied collection of toys should be one of the best ways to encourage long, imaginative play.

Text 2

Occupational therapy researchers at the University of Toledo observed 36 toddlers aged 18 to 30 months during two supervised play sessions: one in a room with four toys and one in a room with sixteen. With fewer toys available, the children switched from toy to toy less often. They also played with each toy for longer periods and used each one in a greater variety of ways.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption discussed in Text 1?
options: Toddlers offered only a few toys tend to lose interest in playing sooner than toddlers offered many.
An abundance of toys may actually work against the kind of focused, inventive play that it is intended to promote.
The kinds of toys available to toddlers influence the quality of their play more than the number of toys does.
Toddlers engage in more imaginative play when a parent joins in than when an adult merely supervises them.
items.explanation: Text 1 presents the assumption that a large, varied collection of toys is one of the best ways to encourage long, imaginative play. The researchers found that toddlers in a room with four toys played with each toy longer and in more ways than they did in a room with sixteen. Their finding suggests that an abundance of toys may work against the very kind of play it is supposed to encourage.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 reports the opposite: with fewer toys, the toddlers played with each toy for longer periods.

C.why_wrong: The study compared numbers of toys, not kinds of toys, so Text 2 gives no basis for ranking type above number.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 mentions supervised sessions only as part of the method; it says nothing about play with a parent joining in.

sources.what: Dauch, Imwalle, Ocasio, Metz 2018, Infant Behavior and Development 50: 36 toddlers, Four Toy and Sixteen Toy conditions; fewer toys gave fewer incidences of toy play, longer play with each toy, more varied play

Text 1

Indigo, the source of the deep blue still used to color denim, has been among the most valued and widespread dyes since antiquity. Because indigo is insoluble in water, dyers must first convert it chemically into a soluble compound that fibers can absorb, a process known as vatting. Exposure to air then restores the characteristic blue. Until recently, <u>textile historians identified ancient Egypt as the site of the dye’s earliest known use, citing textiles with indigo-dyed bands produced about 4,400 years ago</u>.

Text 2

Huaca Prieta, a ceremonial mound on Peru’s northern coast, contains floors buried as deep as 18 meters, where fragments of cotton fabric were preserved for millennia. Analyzing blue yarns from eight of these fabrics, anthropologist Jeffrey Splitstoser and his coauthors detected indigo dye in five. The oldest of the dyed fragments, a blue-striped textile, came from a layer dated to approximately 6,000 years ago.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
options: Egyptian dyers most likely learned the vatting process from textile makers who lived on the coast of South America.
Cotton was cultivated for textiles on the coast of Peru long before it was cultivated in ancient Egypt.
The fabrics from Huaca Prieta were probably dyed with a different plant than the one used for the Egyptian textiles.
People in South America were dyeing fabric with indigo long before the Egyptian textiles were made.
items.explanation: The underlined claim says that the earliest known use of indigo came from Egyptian textiles made about 4,400 years ago. Splitstoser and his coauthors found indigo dye in cotton fabrics from Huaca Prieta, Peru, the oldest of them dated to about 6,000 years ago. So the author of Text 2 would say that people in South America were dyeing fabric with indigo long before the Egyptian textiles were made.

A.why_wrong: Neither text suggests any contact between South American and Egyptian dyers; Text 2 only dates the Peruvian fabrics.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 mentions cotton fabric, but neither text says when cotton was first grown in Peru or in Egypt.

C.why_wrong: Neither text identifies the plant used for either set of textiles, so no comparison of plants is supported.

items.passage:
Text 1

Global poverty statistics are most often reported as counts of people whose income or spending falls below an international poverty line. This threshold, set by the World Bank, is expressed as a fixed amount of money per person per day. The approach has clear strengths. A single money-based measure can be derived from household surveys and compared across countries and decades, allowing analysts to track whether the share of people living in extreme poverty is shrinking.

Text 2

Economist Sabina Alkire, director of the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative, regards income as just one dimension of deprivation. The Multidimensional Poverty Index that she and Maria Emma Santos introduced in 2010 instead records whether households lack schooling, adequate nutrition, clean drinking water, electricity, and other necessities. The results can differ sharply from income-based figures: in Niger, about two-thirds of the population was income poor, but 93 percent was poor by the index’s measure.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Alkire (Text 2) most likely regard the approach to measuring poverty described in Text 1?
options: As incomplete, because a monetary threshold can fail to register many of the hardships that poor households actually experience
As outdated, because the poverty line it relies on has not been adjusted to reflect rising prices
As overly broad, because it classifies as poor many people whose basic needs are adequately met
As impractical, because household surveys are too costly to conduct regularly in many countries
items.explanation: Text 1 describes counting the poor by a single money threshold, the international poverty line. Alkire treats income as only one dimension of deprivation, and her index, which records lacks in schooling, nutrition, water and electricity, found far more people poor in Niger than income figures did. She would therefore regard the income approach as incomplete, since a money threshold can miss many hardships that poor households face.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 does not criticize how the poverty line is adjusted for prices; its point is that income leaves out other deprivations.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 suggests the opposite: in Niger the income measure counted fewer people as poor than the index did.

D.why_wrong: Household surveys are mentioned only in Text 1 as a strength, and Text 2 raises no objection about their cost.

sources.what: Alkire and Santos 2010 OPHI research brief: MPI developed for the 2010 Human Development Report; deprivations in education, health and living standards; goes beyond income; Niger two-thirds income poor vs 93 percent MPI poor
Sabina Alkire, director of OPHI, economist (DPhil in economics, Oxford)

Text 1

Pavement and buildings absorb sunlight and release it as heat, keeping cities warmer than the surrounding countryside. As summers grow hotter, many cities have responded to this urban heat island effect by planting trees, which shade streets and release water vapor through their leaves. Supporters of these programs often assume that <u>every tree planted along a street will make the surrounding neighborhood noticeably cooler</u>.

Text 2

Ecologist Carly Ziter mounted a temperature sensor on her bicycle. Riding ten routes across Madison, Wisconsin, several times each during the summer of 2016, she recorded air temperatures every five meters. Daytime temperatures generally fell as tree canopy cover increased, but the relationship was far from linear. The greatest cooling occurred where the canopy covered more than 40 percent of the surrounding area, roughly the size of a city block.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Ziter (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim underlined in Text 1?
options: By arguing that reducing pavement would cool city blocks more effectively than planting trees would
By pointing out that trees lower temperatures on city streets more at night than during the day
By noting that a few added trees may do little to cool a block unless its canopy cover reaches a certain level
By recommending that cities measure air temperatures along each street before choosing which trees to plant
items.explanation: The underlined claim says that every tree planted along a street makes the neighborhood noticeably cooler. Ziter found that daytime cooling did not rise steadily with canopy cover: the greatest cooling occurred only where canopy covered more than 40 percent of an area about the size of a city block. She would therefore say that a few added trees may do little unless canopy cover reaches that kind of level.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 reports only how canopy cover relates to temperature; it does not compare tree planting with removing pavement.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 describes daytime temperatures only and says nothing about cooling at night.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 does not discuss which trees to plant or recommend any planning step.

Text 1

Over the past two centuries, the average height of people in the Netherlands has risen by about 20 centimeters, and the Dutch are now among the tallest people in the world. A change this rapid is generally attributed to the environment rather than to genes. Scientists have credited better diets and medical care, which allowed each new generation of Dutch children to come closer to its full growth potential.

Text 2

Demographer Gert Stulp analyzed data from a large health study of people in the northern Netherlands born between 1935 and 1967. Among the men in the study, the taller ones had more children, on average, than the shorter ones did. Because height is highly heritable, Stulp proposes that this difference in reproductive success may have gradually pushed the Dutch population toward greater stature.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Stulp (Text 2) most likely respond to the explanation presented in Text 1?
options: By suggesting that natural selection, along with better living conditions, may have made the Dutch taller
By arguing that Dutch women have gained more height over the same period than Dutch men have
By claiming that improvements in diet had little effect on the height of people in the northern Netherlands
By noting that Dutch men born after 1967 are, on average, no taller than those born earlier
items.explanation: Text 1 explains the rise in Dutch height by environmental improvements in diet and medical care. Stulp found that taller men had more children and, since height is heritable, proposes that this pushed the population toward greater height, which is natural selection. He would add this cause to the environmental one rather than reject it.

B.why_wrong: Neither text compares how much height women and men gained over the period.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 proposes an additional cause; it never denies that better diets mattered.

D.why_wrong: The year 1967 marks the end of the study’s birth range; Text 2 says nothing about the height of people born later.

Text 1

Women experience adverse reactions to medications nearly twice as often as men do. Researchers Irving Zucker and Brian Prendergast trace much of this disparity to dosing. Reviewing studies of 86 drugs approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), they found that for 76, women given the same dose as men had higher concentrations of the drug in their blood or eliminated it more slowly. Because most drugs in use were approved on the basis of trials conducted on men, the researchers argue, women are routinely overmedicated.

Text 2

When the FDA approved the sleep medication zolpidem in 1992, women and men were prescribed the same 10-milligram dose. Over the following decades, reports accumulated of patients who remained drowsy the morning after taking the drug, sometimes while driving. In 2013, <u>the FDA cut the recommended dose for women in half, explaining that women clear zolpidem from their bodies more slowly than men do</u>.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Zucker and Prendergast (Text 1) most likely regard the situation presented in the underlined portion of Text 2?
options: As surprising, because zolpidem was among the few drugs tested extensively on women before it was approved
As predictable, because a dose that suits men often leaves women with more of a drug in their blood than intended
As premature, because the FDA had received only a small number of reports of drowsiness from patients
As overly cautious, because the morning effects of zolpidem are explained by body weight rather than by sex
items.explanation: Zucker and Prendergast found that women given the same dose as men often end up with higher concentrations of a drug in their blood or eliminate it more slowly, so standard doses tend to overmedicate women. The zolpidem case in Text 2 fits that pattern exactly: a shared dose was later halved for women because they clear the drug more slowly. They would therefore regard the FDA’s change as predictable.

A.why_wrong: Text 1 says most drugs were approved on the basis of trials on men, and nothing suggests zolpidem was an exception.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 says reports accumulated over decades, and Text 1’s findings would support lowering the dose, not delaying it.

D.why_wrong: Text 1 attributes women’s higher drug levels to sex differences in how drugs are processed, not to body weight, and argues that women are overmedicated.

sources.what: Zucker and Prendergast 2020, Biology of Sex Differences: women experience adverse drug reactions nearly twice as often; 86 drugs, 76 with higher pharmacokinetic values in women; most drugs approved on trials conducted on men; women may be overmedicated; zolpidem cited as an illustrative example, approved by the FDA one year before the 1993 NIH Revitalization Act

items.passage:
Text 1

Dutch painter Rachel Ruysch (1664–1750) grew up surrounded by the natural world in preserved form. Her father, the anatomist and botanist Frederik Ruysch, kept a celebrated collection of specimens, from which she learned to draw as a girl, and at fifteen she began training with the flower painter Willem van Aelst. In her still lifes, insects and snails crawl among blossoms rendered petal by petal. These works read almost as botanical records, capturing the plants of her day with a naturalist’s care.

Text 2

Rachel Ruysch’s flower paintings should not be treated simply as records of what the artist saw. Ruysch must in some cases have worked from preserved specimens, as art historian Stephanie Dickey notes. Yet her bouquets combine plants that bloom in different places and seasons, arranged in color harmonies that could never have existed at a single moment. The paintings, in Dickey’s view, are also feats of deceptive artifice.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
options: Ruysch’s bouquets reproduce arrangements of flowers that she actually assembled in her studio.
Ruysch learned more about depicting flowers from Willem van Aelst than from her father.
Ruysch’s paintings were valued more highly in her lifetime than those of most Dutch artists.
Ruysch’s paintings drew in part on her study of preserved specimens.
items.explanation: Text 1 says Ruysch learned to draw from her father’s collection of specimens and painted plants with a naturalist’s care. The author of Text 2 argues that her bouquets are invented arrangements but accepts, with Dickey, that in some cases Ruysch must have worked from preserved specimens. Both authors would therefore agree that her paintings drew in part on her study of preserved specimens.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 rejects this: the bouquets combine plants from different places and seasons that could never have been arranged together.

B.why_wrong: Only Text 1 mentions both her father and van Aelst, and it never says which taught her more.

C.why_wrong: Neither text discusses the prices or reputation of Ruysch’s paintings compared with other artists’ work.

Text 1

Many sleep researchers have warned that people in industrialized countries are chronically sleep deprived. Electric lighting allows activity to continue long after sunset; televisions, computers, and phones further delay bedtime; and alarm clocks fix the hour of waking. Before these technologies became widespread, people presumably went to bed soon after dark and slept much longer each night than most people do today.

Text 2

A team including anthropologist Gandhi Yetish and sleep researcher Jerome Siegel used wrist-worn devices to monitor the sleep of members of three preindustrial societies that lack electric lighting: the Hadza of Tanzania, the San of the Kalahari Desert, and the Tsimane of Bolivia. On average, participants did not fall asleep until more than three hours after sunset. They slept between 5.7 and 7.1 hours a night—amounts near the low end of those reported for industrialized societies.
items.stem: Which choice best describes a difference in how the author of Text 1 and the author of Text 2 view sleep among people who lack modern technologies such as electric lighting?
options: The author of Text 1 attributes such people’s sleep patterns to the timing of sunset, whereas the author of Text 2 attributes them mainly to the demands of work.
The author of Text 1 believes that such people nap more often during the day than the author of Text 2 believes they do.
The author of Text 1 assumes that such people sleep longer than people in industrialized societies, whereas the author of Text 2 presents evidence that they do not.
The author of Text 1 relies on measurements of sleep in industrialized countries, whereas the author of Text 2 relies on people’s own reports of how long they slept.
items.explanation: The author of Text 1 holds that before electric lighting and other technologies, people presumably went to bed soon after dark and slept much longer than people do today. Text 2 reports that members of three societies without electric lighting slept 5.7 to 7.1 hours, near the low end for industrialized societies. So the two authors differ on whether such people sleep longer than people in industrialized societies.

A.why_wrong: Text 1 does link bedtime to darkness, but Text 2 never attributes sleep patterns to the demands of work.

D.why_wrong: Text 1 cites no measurements, and Text 2 relies on wrist-worn devices, not on people’s own reports.

items.passage:
Text 1

Ethnographic studies of recent hunter-gatherer societies have documented a striking regularity: men typically hunt large game, while women gather plants. Many anthropologists have treated this pattern as a window onto the deep past. In their view, such a division of labor by sex is ancestral to our species, and <u>big-game hunting in the earliest hunter-gatherer societies was an exclusively male pursuit</u>.

Text 2

In 2018, archaeologist Randall Haas and colleagues excavated a 9,000-year-old burial at Wilamaya Patjxa, a site in the Andean highlands of Peru. Buried with this individual was a toolkit of stone projectile points and implements for processing animal carcasses—equipment associated with hunting large animals. Skeletal features and sex-specific proteins preserved in tooth enamel indicated that this hunter was a young woman. Surveying early burials throughout the Americas, the team identified ten other females buried with comparable hunting equipment.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
options: Patterns observed in recent hunter-gatherer societies may not reveal who hunted large game in early ones.
Big-game hunting was more common in the Andean highlands than in other parts of the Americas during the same period.
Women in early hunter-gatherer societies probably hunted large animals more often than the men in those societies did.
Ethnographers have exaggerated how frequently men in recent hunter-gatherer societies take part in hunting large game.
items.explanation: The underlined claim, drawn from the pattern in recent hunter-gatherer societies, is that big-game hunting in the earliest societies was done only by men. Haas and colleagues found a 9,000-year-old female buried with a big-game hunting toolkit and ten other early females buried with similar equipment. They would conclude that the pattern seen in recent societies may not show who hunted large game in early ones.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 does not compare how common hunting was in the Andes with other regions.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 shows that some early females hunted large game, not that women hunted it more often than men.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 challenges the inference about early societies, not the ethnographic reports about recent ones.

Text 1

The narwhal’s spiraled tusk is an elongated canine tooth projecting from the left side of the upper jaw. In 2014, dental researcher Martin Nweeia reported that the tusk’s porous outer layer admits seawater into microscopic tubules connected to nerves in its core. When his team alternately exposed the tusks of live narwhals to salty and fresh water, the animals’ heart rates changed. The tusk, Nweeia proposed, functions as a sensory organ.

Text 2

An organ essential for sensing the environment would be expected in both sexes, yet tusks are nearly universal among male narwhals and rare among females. Analyzing measurements of 245 adult males collected over 35 years, biologist Zackary Graham found that tusk length increased disproportionately with body size and varied far more among similarly sized males than did the width of the tail flukes—patterns characteristic of sexually selected traits.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the hypothesis about the narwhal tusk presented in Text 1?
options: By questioning whether the tubules in the tusk are actually connected to nerves
By suggesting that the tusk is used mainly to locate prey rather than to detect changes in salinity
By arguing that it leaves unexplained why the tusk is largely restricted to males and grows disproportionately long in larger ones
By agreeing that the tusk is a sensory organ but suggesting that female narwhals depend on it less than males do
items.explanation: Text 1 presents Nweeia’s hypothesis that the tusk is a sensory organ. The author of Text 2 points out that a sensory organ should appear in both sexes, yet tusks are rare in females, and cites Graham’s finding that tusk length grows disproportionately with body size, as sexually selected traits do. The author would therefore say the sensory hypothesis leaves both of these patterns unexplained.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 does not dispute the anatomy described in Text 1; it questions what the tusk is for.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 does not propose any sensory use, such as finding prey; it argues for a role in competition among males.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 does not accept that the tusk is a sensory organ; it uses the tusk’s rarity in females against that idea.

In 1982, consumer researchers Joel Huber, John Payne, and Christopher Puto showed that adding a third option to a choice set can shift preferences between the original two.
